ReNailed
Pull the nails. Keep the wood. Build it again. ReNailed turns clean, short old-growth wood that the reuse market rejects into bolted public benches, tagged with the house the wood came from.

01
The story starts on a Vancouver street
A 1930s house comes down. Inside it is old-growth wood.
“Most pre 1950 homes are built of old growth lumber,” says the City of Vancouver. The wood is valuable; the labour and paperwork are the barrier.
13,005 kg
of lumber in one Grandview-Woodland house
160 hours
spent just pulling the nails out of it
$15,310
demolition deposit, refunded only with recycling receipts
Sources: CoV, Grandview-Woodland case study; CoV, demolition permit and compliance review.

Q1
Q&A 1 of 7 · Questions 1–5
Business idea and competitive advantage
1 · Why hasn’t a lumber yard done this?
Yards sell volume lumber; Urbanjacks glues short pieces into 20-ft boards. Installed, serviced seating is a small niche. We’d rather supply them (Choi).
2 · Does a 6-ft rule prove no market?
No. Flooring uses 3-ft pieces (Teshnizi). Our claim: buyers aren’t absorbing it; Riley Park still burned 74% of its lumber (CoV).
3 · What stops a copycat?
The design is copyable. Contractor access, City-ready receipts, per-piece data and maintenance contracts take years (CoV). Best case: they buy our slats.
4 · Recovery or furniture first?
Furniture. Wood is ≈ $29 of $3,500, so benches work with bought wood (MV). Recovery alone needs ≥ $549 per saleable tonne [C] (CoV).
5 · Why not just sell short boards?
De-nailed 2×4 sells for $0.25–0.30/ft (Teshnizi); 26 kg ≈ $29 of wood becomes a $3,500 bench [T]. Selling slats is our fallback.
Our one-line edge
Upstream access to clean, traceable old growth, turned into a product cities already buy.
Sources: City of Richmond (2024); Burnaby Now; SFU Procurement; Teshnizi (2015).
Q2
Q&A 2 of 7 · Questions 6–10
Customers and willingness to pay
6 · Who has agreed to pay $3,500?
No one yet. $3,500 is proposed [T], set at Richmond’s fee; Surrey $2,800–3,800; Burnaby’s real cost $5,000. First milestone: a signed letter of intent.
7 · If SFU facilities says no?
Budget holder, facilities and Procurement must all agree; under $10,000 needs only a requisition (SFU). If no: a private buyer who holds all three roles.
8 · Why not a cheaper normal bench?
Repair, not replace: one slat unbolts. Upkeep priced up front (Burnaby budgets $200/yr); reused content counts for LEED, up to 4 points (Teshnizi).
9 · Is Burnaby’s $5,000 a fair compare?
Not yet: it bundles bench and install, upkeep separate (Burnaby Now). We’ll price ours and two supplier quotes on one scope sheet.
10 · If campus takes a year?
One bench is far below SFU’s $50,000 bidding threshold. Meanwhile we sell to cafés, neighbourhood houses, gardens, stratas.
Verified willingness to pay: $0
We say it plainly. Dedication fees are donations, not purchases; an LOI is our proof.
Sources: CoV Grandview-Woodland; MV case studies; USDA Wood Handbook; Burnaby Now; Gov. of BC; MV clean-wood card.
Q3
Q&A 3 of 7 · Questions 11–16
Financial questions
11 · Is cheap wood an advantage?
No. Our edge is early access to clean, traceable old growth (CoV) plus the receipts contractors need for their deposit.
12 · Does $30 include rejects?
$29 is recovered-lumber value (MV). De-nailing is in labour; at 60% yield wood is $49; collection adds $100 [T]. Nothing counted twice.
13 · Why trust the base case?
Tested: wood mass, value, de-nail time. Untested: price, frame, hours. Surrey’s $2,800 low end beats the $2,500 downside.
14 · Is overhead counted twice?
No. Per bench $300 = $150 engineering + $150 warranty. Overhead sits only in $10,000 fixed [T]: 7 benches, 8 fully loaded [C].
15 · With every hour paid?
+6 h admin ($150) and $100 collection: $2,230 cost, +$1,270 at $3,500, +$570 at $2,800 [C]. We pay $25/h vs $18.25 minimum (Gov BC).
16 · Who funds maintenance later?
$150 warranty reserve held per bench; upkeep sold separately (Burnaby: $200/yr). Worn slats go to clean-wood recycling (MV).
Sources: IRC R507.7; AWC DCA 6; USDA Wood Handbook; Teshnizi (2015); Falk & Green (1999); CWC; CoV; US Access Board, ADA 903.
Q4
Q&A 4 of 7 · Questions 17–21
Design and operations
17 · A 4-ft board in a 6-ft bench?
Supports every 2 ft; rows are one 6-ft piece or 4 + 2 ft, staggered. 5.2 vs 15.7 MPa unsupported [C]; decks allow 24 in (IRC).
18 · Backed or backless?
Backless, ≈ 26 kg [C]. Accessible benches need back support (ADA 903.4): then the backed model leads.
19 · How do slats stay consistent?
USDA method: nail holes graded as knots. Accept ≤ 19% moisture (CWC), mill to one size, 1/8-in gaps for ≈ 2 mm swelling [C]. Plan 50% rejects.
20 · Wood tomorrow, no orders?
We decline; demolition goes ahead as planned. Buyer-first, one-pallet buffer; the required hazardous-materials report gives us lead time (CoV).
21 · Does $300 cover bench #1?
No. It’s a batch figure. Prototype engineering and testing are a one-time startup cost; the USDA lab tested to ASTM D198.
Stiffness check [C]
1,500 N mid-slat: ≈ 0.5 mm sag on a 2-ft gap [C]. ADA 903.6 requires 250 lb (1,112 N); we test above it.
Sources: Tetra Tech (2026); Teshnizi (2015); MV directory; CoV Riley Park; worldsteel (2024); MV clean-wood card.
Q5
Q&A 5 of 7 · Questions 22–25
Environmental impact and credibility
Our impact rule
Reuse, recycling, energy recovery and disposal are reported separately; we count only weighed wood with no other buyer.
22 · Is 2.6 t meaningful?
Alone, no: ≈ 0.0015% of 174,241 t of wood [C] (Tetra Tech). Benches make 4–6 ft pieces pay; scale is the 1,000–1,500 t of salvageable lumber a year via Sort & Supply (Teshnizi).
23 · Prove it would be discarded?
Per lot: permit type, disposal receipts, pieces below ReStore’s 6-ft minimum (MV), no buyer bid. Baseline: Riley Park burned 74% (CoV). Reported as “probable additional”.
24 · Does new steel cancel it out?
Possibly. Steel averages 1.92 t CO₂ per tonne (worldsteel); a 25 kg frame [T] ≈ 48 kg CO₂ [C]. So we make no carbon claim until a life-cycle study.
25 · “Never thrown away”?
Removed. Worn slats go to clean-wood recycling (MV); steel is reused or scrapped; the tag links an open spec so anyone can re-slat.
Sources: our model [C]; Burnaby Now; CoV Dunbar case study; Teshnizi (2015) framing per house.
Q6
Q&A 6 of 7 · Questions 26–28
Final pressure questions
26 · What result makes you stop?
Any one of: no buyer at ≥ $2,230 in five talks; build over 24 h; load test fails; 4–6 ft share under 5% of a house [C]. Pivot: sell graded slats to makers.
27 · Funded today, what first?
Willingness to pay. Success: one letter of intent at ≥ $2,800, Surrey’s low end (Burnaby Now), for a bench built in ≤ 12 h that passes the load check.
28 · Why not fund an existing yard?
We feed them: 6 ft+ wood goes to buyers like Western Reclaimed and Heritage Lumber, who bought Dunbar’s lumber (CoV). If a yard can do benches cheaper, we supply it.
Sources: Falk & Green (1999); CWC; BIFMA X5.4; USDA Wood Handbook; Teshnizi (2015); Health Canada; Arbelaez et al. (2019).
Q7
Q&A 7 of 7 · Questions 29–32
Prototyping and material engineering
Durability note
Douglas-fir is “moderately resistant to decay” (Wood Handbook): wood stays off the ground, slats drain, and worn slats are replaced.
29 · What will the prototype test?
Grade (USDA method) → moisture ≤ 19% (CWC) → proof-load slats on a 2-ft span, ASTM D198 as reference → bench load and stability (BIFMA X5.4 checklist) → one outdoor season.
30 · How strong is salvaged wood?
Clear fir ≈ 85 MPa (Wood Handbook); salvaged ~25% weaker (Teshnizi); recycled 2×4s average one grade lower (Falk & Green). Our grid keeps stress ≈ 5 MPa [C]. Seating only.
31 · How do you keep out toxic wood?
Screened twice: the City’s hazardous-materials report, then the Lab. Reject paint (pre-1960 lead risk) and pre-2004 deck or fence wood, likely CCA (Health Canada).
32 · Enough consistent slats?
In Portland, 267 of 483 salvaged 2×4s were under 2.3 m (Arbelaez). Our 2, 4 and 6-ft cuts use most pieces of 4 ft or more; one-house length tally confirms.

Q&A backup · questions from the stakeholder map
Access, process, build, maintain
1 · How will we access the wood?
Pre-demolition survey with the contractor’s consent. Pre-1950 houses need 75–90% reuse or recycling and a $15,310 deposit refunded only with receipts (CoV), and disposal costs $124–194/t (CoV; MV). We remove clean wood free and hand back receipts.
2 · How will we process it?
In the De-Nail Lab: metal-scan, pull nails, grade nail holes as knots (Falk & Green), accept ≤ 19% moisture (CWC), mill. Benchmark: 160 h for 7.15 t reused (CoV), ≈ 35 min per bench [C]. Kit ≈ US$2,670.
3 · Who will build and install it?
We assemble slats on a local fabricator’s steel frame [T]; an engineer load-checks the 2-ft grid (IRC spacing as guide); an installer anchors it. RX Made in Chicago already builds benches from reclaimed wood (Metropolis).
4 · How will we maintain it?
Bolted slats swap out. Plans priced like Burnaby’s $200 per bench per year (Burnaby Now) plus a $150 warranty reserve [T]. Fir is “moderately resistant to decay” (Wood Handbook), so slats drain and worn ones are recycled (MV).
